description: Computer Engineering students at Birzeit University using space data to solve problems close to home. We’re working on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data Challenge. We bring machine learning, data analysis, Python, MATLAB, and Android/Spring Boot app development.
summary: Ardi (أرضي) is a mobile app that helps farmers decide what to plant, when to sow, and how much to water, using real NASA data. It is built first for Palestine, with NASA data for all 12 governorates, and it also covers areas in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Turkey. Farmers usually sow “around” a traditional date, but the rain has changed. Ardi uses 26 years of NASA POWER daily data (2000–2025) to give each field an exact sowing window. It compares the farmer’s own plan with the two best NASA-based plans by water need, soil health and risk, and gives weekly irrigation advice. Farmers can ask questions by voice in a WhatsApp-style chat, in Arabic (including Palestinian dialect) or English. For chickpea in Jenin, sowing on 17–19 January instead of mid-February cut water-short seasons from 67% to 21%.
details:
Ardi (أرضي, “my land”) is a bilingual Arabic/English web app that turns NASA climate data into a season plan for the small rain-fed farmer in Palestine and the wider region. A farmer signs up with their phone number. They enter their land once: country, town and climate area, plus water source (rain-fed, supplemental or irrigated), land use (commercial, home or both) and area in dunums. Then they tell Ardi what they plan to grow this season and what they grew in the two seasons before.

What it does

  • Compares three plans side by side. Ardi puts the farmer’s own plan next to the two best NASA-data plans for that land. Each plan gets a fit score out of 100, a sowing window, season length and harvest date, water needs and shortfall in m³ for the whole field, rain coverage, expected yield, market return, effect on soil, crop-rotation fit, and the crop to grow next season. If the farmer hasn’t decided yet, Ardi shows the three best options.
  • Gives sowing dates that get more precise over time. When the window is months away, it says “mid-February”. Within three weeks it narrows to exact days.
  • Gives weekly guidance. Each land page answers “what do I do this week?”: when to sow, the irrigation need for the whole field, and a 5-day forecast with frost, heat, heavy-rain and wind alerts.
  • Sends alerts by WhatsApp or SMS.
  • Gives the Ministry of Agriculture a dashboard. It shows anonymous, aggregated data by area, and only from farmers who opt in.

How it works

  • The engine scores each crop on four things: germination temperature, frost risk, heat at flowering, and rain versus crop water demand.
  • It uses FAO-56 crop coefficients and reference evapotranspiration, so water needs are calculated, not guessed.
  • It adjusts each score for the farmer’s goal, soil condition, rotation history and land use.
  • The design is built around NASA POWER daily variables: temperature, precipitation, humidity and evapotranspiration inputs.
  • The current prototype runs on approximate monthly climate data for 17 areas in Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Turkey. Connecting the live NASA POWER feed per area is the next step.

Benefits and intended impact

  • The problem: 68.7% of Palestinian farm holdings receive no agricultural extension service, there are only 218 extension officers, and 83.8% of farmers own a smartphone.
  • Better decisions: Ardi gives farmers evidence-based advice on their phone, in Arabic, about what to sow, when, and how much water it will take.
  • Real gains: it helps farmers sow at the right time in drier, shifting seasons, avoid repeating crops, save irrigation water, and improve their soil.
  • For the ministry: a real-time picture of what is planted where, without sharing any farmer’s identity.

Tools used

  • The app: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, as a single-page app with no framework. It works offline after loading and on any phone browser.
  • Build and testing: a Python build script and Node.js tests for the agronomic engine.
  • Pitch and branding: Canva.
  • Methods: NASA POWER as the climate data source and FAO-56 for crop water requirements.

How it’s creative

  • The comparison: most tools hand the farmer an answer. Ardi starts from the farmer’s own decision and shows, with numbers, how it compares to two alternatives. Farmers keep control and learn why.
  • Water in field terms: it gives water in cubic metres for the whole field, a unit farmers can act on, instead of millimetres.
  • Honest timing: it only commits to exact sowing days when the forecast can support it.

Factors we considered

  • What farmers already know: we consulted a local agricultural engineer. He told us farmers already know not to sow the same crop twice, so Ardi adds data, not lessons.
  • Access: there is little direct contact between advisers and farmers in Palestine, so Ardi works through the phone and links to the ministry.
  • Inclusion: Arabic first, simple screens, sign-in by phone code instead of passwords, and support for home gardens as well as commercial land.
  • Privacy: sharing data with the ministry is opt-in and anonymous.
  • Honesty about limits: NASA POWER is about 50 km resolution, and the crop table still needs review by an agronomist. Our next steps are Sentinel-2/WaPOR field-level data, agronomist review, and field testing with farmers in Jenin.
